newsitem.title: CROATIA: All set for polls in Serb enclave, UN chief says.
newsitem.headline: All set for polls in Serb enclave, UN chief says.

text.p: The U.N. administrator of the last Serb enclave in Croatia, due to revert to government rule soon, said on Thursday all preconditions were met for holding crucial post-war elections there on Sunday.

"I think all in all everything that could be done has been done...All the preconditions for elections are in place," U.S general Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. administration of Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), told a news conference.
"Now it's simply the matter of the people in the region taking the matter into their own hands and chosing for themselves," he told reporters after meeting Croatian president Franjo Tudjman.

The voting, conciding with the countrywide regional and local polls, will include Eastern Slavonia for the first time since it rebelled against Croatia's independence and formed its own state in 1991.
The Serbs, linked with rebel kin in two other breakaway enclaves inside Croatia, expelled over 80,000 non-Serbs from the fertile, oil-producing Eastern Slavonia.
But Croatia recaptured the other two enclaves in 1995 and negotiated a peaceful "reintegration" of Eastern Slavonia, now monitored by some 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers whose mandate expires on July 15.

The U.N. and Croatian authorities have agreed to allow all the eligible Serbs, including thousands of Serb refugees from other enclave to vote on Sunday, on condition they apply for Croatian citizenship papers.

The UNTAES even stretched the deadline for their registration until Saturday, less than 24 hours before the polls would open, "so no one can say the U.N. did not do everything possible to give everyone time and chance to register and thus excercise their political will".

On Sunday 69,500 Croat refugees scattered across the country will cast their ballots against 71,500 or possibly more Serbs now in the enclave. Only a "symbolic" number of the Croats will cross the U.N- patrolled lines to vote.
Klein said UNTAES was making every effort to ensure the voting is done in a safe and fair manner.
"On Sunday we'll have all our 5,000 peacekeepers with their vehicles out on the streets and UNTAES monitors will be in every polling place," he said.

But he stressed that despite international and Croatian appeals and guarantees of safety and minority rights, a number of Serbs refused to apply for Croatian papers, dismissing the reintegration and life under Croatian rule.

"There are people who don't want peaceful reintegration to work but we can't sympthatise with them because they are trying to undermine our mission -- to give Serbs of the region a future in the Croatian state," he said.
